title: Indian Green Card Holder Says He Would Not Move to the US on an H-1B Today
excerpt: Mohamed Zeeshan bypassed the H-1B lottery by self-petitioning for a green card from abroad, but says the growing uncertainty around US immigration makes him worry for those who lack alternatives.
body:
• Mohamed Zeeshan, a 32-year-old Indian national, secured a green card through self-petition in 2023 after bypassing the H-1B pathway
  • Zeeshan says he was drawn to the US for its free speech and entrepreneurial culture, not economic upliftment
  • He warns that growing uncertainty around visa policies and rising denial rates for EB-1A petitions are pushing immigrants toward other countries

Mohamed Zeeshan moved to the United States as a permanent resident in 2023. But if he had to rely on an H-1B visa to get here today, he says he would not do it.

In a first-person account published by Business Insider, the 32-year-old Indian national and green card holder described a winding immigration path that took him from Columbia University to the Middle East and back — and explained why today’s visa landscape feels more hostile than ever for aspiring immigrants.

A Non-Linear Path to Permanent Residency

Zeeshan arrived in the US in 2016 to pursue a master’s in international affairs at Columbia. After graduating in 2018, he hoped to stay through Optional Practical Training (OPT) and eventually transition to an H-1B visa — the route many international students take.

But changes in immigration rhetoric after the 2016 election made employers wary. “I felt that employers were unwilling to take a risk on an international student like me,” he told Business Insider. Rather than wait for an uncertain H-1B lottery, he left the US for a management consulting job in Dubai.

In 2021, Zeeshan pursued an alternative: self-petitioning for a green card from abroad using the EB-2 National Interest Waiver pathway. He submitted extensive evidence of his work in research and public-interest issues, and the petition was approved in 2023.

Drawn by Values, Not Economics

Unlike many immigrants, Zeeshan says economic upliftment was not his primary motivation. He earned more in Dubai, where he paid no income tax, than in his first US job after receiving the green card.

“I was drawn to American ideals of free speech — the ability to write and speak freely about issues, even if they’re controversial.”

— Mohamed Zeeshan, green card holder and author

Zeeshan, who has written a book about India as an emerging power, said he felt freer to critique policymaking in the US than in India, where he is Muslim in a Hindu-majority country. In 2025, he started his own consulting firm in the US, citing less bureaucratic regulation for entrepreneurs.

Growing Uncertainty for H-1B Workers

While Zeeshan found an alternative route, he says the traditional H-1B pathway has become even more fraught. The visa ties workers to a single employer, and losing a job triggers a 60-day countdown to leave the country.

Recent policy changes have compounded the anxiety. A proposed $100,000 H-1B fee was introduced and later struck down by a federal judge, but remains tied up in courts. Data also shows rising denial rates for EB-1A visas, another pathway for skilled immigrants.

Zeeshan says friends and relatives in India are increasingly looking at Germany, Australia, and other destinations because landing a US job and visa after graduating has become significantly harder.

What This Means for Indian Immigrants

Zeeshan’s account lands at a time when the Indian diaspora — the largest H-1B visa recipient group — faces an increasingly uncertain immigration landscape. His wife is still waiting for her own green card, and the couple has delayed having children to minimize uncertainty about her status.

He intends to naturalize and become a US citizen, “unless something makes that difficult.” But his bottom line is clear: if he had to start the process today on an H-1B, he would not take the risk.
nri_angle: An Indian national who self-petitioned for a green card warns that growing H-1B uncertainty is pushing Indian immigrants to consider other countries.
author: Diaspora Desk
